rows.description: A child pushes an adult's hand away from the shoelaces and insists on tying them alone, taking pride in choosing and doing; the wish for independence grows from here.

rows.subtype: Wants to choose own subject and friends [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager wants to choose their stream and friends on their own judgment, and clashes with parents' plans; independence feels like part of who they are.

rows.subtype: Forging own path despite family pressure [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult explores an unusual career, accepting risk and disapproval; freedom and curiosity matter more to them than an approved route, though they still love their family.
A child given a long list of instructions forgets most of them. Working memory holds only a few items, so clear, short steps help.
A teenager who studies with a phone buzzing and music with lyrics finds concepts do not stick, because attention and memory are overloaded.
A student juggling exams, work and worries makes careless mistakes and feels foggy. Mental capacity is limited and stress uses part of it.
A teenager on a scooter is stopped by police and asked for papers, feeling nervous and unsure. Staying calm, being polite, carrying documents and calling a parent are sensible.

A young adult hesitates to file a police complaint over theft or harassment, expecting delay or blame. Going with a trusted person, writing details and seeking legal aid or a senior officer if refused are valid steps.

A young person, especially from a poor, minority or lower-caste background, feels talked down to or threatened. Recording facts, involving family, lawyers or human-rights groups, and staying calm are safer than resisting physically.

rows.subtype: At least it was not worse [Actor]
rows.description: A child who broke a window says it is nothing compared with what the older kids did; comparing with worse acts makes the wrongdoing look small.
A teenager who lies to parents says at least they are not taking drugs like some of their friends; the comparison stretches the moral scale until the act seems minor.

rows.subtype: Cutting corners because the rest do worse [Actor]
rows.description: A student who pays for a ghostwritten assignment says others buy whole degrees; the bar is set by the worst example and not by the person's own values.

rows.subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
rows.description: A child notices which children sit apart, whose parents work in the house and whose name gets teased. Children see difference early; how adults explain it shapes fairness or prejudice.

rows.subtopic: Caste and class awareness, discrimination recognition and fair conduct
rows.description: A young adult hears heated arguments over quotas and merit, and feels drawn to angry slogans. Listening to lived experience and to data, and staying respectful, is wiser than picking a tribe.
A child giggles at funny faces, wrong words and sudden surprises. Early humour is about incongruity and safety, and laughing together bonds a child to a caregiver.
A child repeats the same joke ten times and finds bodily humour hilarious. Testing jokes teaches timing and audience, and groans from listeners are useful feedback.
A teenager uses sarcasm, memes and inside jokes to bond with peers. Shared humour signals who is in the group, and it can also be used to exclude others.
